Notation and Package Conventions

Source: vignettes/notation-and-conventions.Rmd
notation-and-conventions.Rmd

Purpose

RdistNN uses the notation of its companion papers where that notation has a direct computational meaning. This article collects the translation in one place. It is intended to answer three questions that otherwise recur across help pages:

  1. Which mathematical object does a package argument represent?
  2. Is the object supplied by the user, computed by the package, or merely retained as a diagnostic?
  3. Does an uncertainty field describe a localized moment or an estimated target coefficient?

The notation is shared across several estimators, but the estimators do not all perform the same operation. In particular, np_dnn() and cate_dnn() localize scalar signals, the experimental plqr_dnn() evaluates a vector moment at a supplied coefficient, and the experimental gmm_dnn() front end solves a local moment problem.

This is the collection’s crosswalk and navigation article. It explains notation and conventions that cut across estimators; the linked articles remain the authoritative source for complete workflows, diagnostics, extension patterns, and paper-specific replication.

How the vignette collection fits together

The vignette collection has four complementary layers:

  1. Start with the package tour and the common DNN localization machinery.
  2. Move to an estimator article for the NP and CATE workflows or experimental PLQR and IV details.
  3. Consult the diagnostics and visualization articles when interpreting a fit.
  4. Use the extension and replication articles only when you need those more specialized interfaces.

This article sits between those layers. Return here when a symbol or field has different meanings in two workflows, or when it is unclear whether an object is an input, an intermediate quantity, a diagnostic, or an inferential output.

Names vary slightly when R object conventions require it. For example, plqr_result uses neff, whereas a requested common weight diagnostic is called ess. These fields represent the same inverse-Herfindahl effective sample size when the weight columns are normalized.

Localization and DNN conventions

Training covariates and targets

X is the n×pn\times p matrix used to rank observations around a target. The package uses x0 for one length-pp target and X0 for an M×pM\times p matrix of targets. Supply exactly one of x0 and X0. Internally, both are resolved to a target matrix whose rows index evaluation points.

In the data-frame interface, x_cols selects the columns that form X. The values in x0 or rows of X0 must follow that same column order. When column names are available, fitted objects retain them in the returned x0 matrix.

The localization state XX need not equal the full adjustment state used by a nuisance function. The conditional Z-estimation paper often writes U=(X,Z)U=(X,Z). The package localizes on X, while supplied nuisances such as PLQR g and mD may have been estimated using the larger state UU.

Kernel order s and neighbor count k

The two integer controls have different jobs:

  • s is the DNN kernel order. In the complete-statistic interpretation, it is the subsample size over which the nearest-neighbor kernel is averaged.
  • k is the number of nearest observations selected inside each size-s subsample. The companion paper’s stated theory uses the default k = 1L.

Consequently, s is not an ordinary request to keep the nearest s observations. Exact DNN weights can have support beyond rank s; for fixed k, their finite-sample support reaches rank n - s + k. The optional neighbors return records the first k observations used inside a subsample, not the complete support of the averaged DNN weight vector.

When s is omitted, tuning_dnn_paper() supplies the paper rule

s=⌊λsn(kx+1)/(kx+2)⌋, s = \left\lfloor \lambda_s n^{(k_x+1)/(k_x+2)} \right\rfloor,

with package argument lambda, default value 0.4, and kx=dim⁡(X)k_x=\dim(X) unless kx_override is set. The argument is called lambda rather than kappa so it does not collide with unrelated uses of κ\kappa in the theory.

Weights and effective sample size

For one target, let wi(x)w_i(x) denote the normalized DNN weight on observation ii. For multiple targets, W[i, j] is wi(xj)w_i(x_j). With normalized weights,

neff(x)={∑i=1nwi(x)2}−1. n_{\mathrm{eff}}(x) = \left\{\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(x)^2\right\}^{-1}.

The same quantity appears under three public names:

  • ess when requested as a common weight extra;
  • neff in PLQR and GMM result objects;
  • n_eff in tidy diagnostics and paper-facing reporting.

It is a weight-concentration measure, not a count of nonzero weights. Physical radius diagnostics answer a different question: how far from x0 one must move to collect a specified fraction of weight mass.

Continue with DNN weights for the weight algorithms and returned rank diagnostics, or kernel-order tuning for the tuning rule and candidate-grid workflow.

Matrix and data-frame interfaces

High-level estimators support two outer interfaces. The data-frame interface is usually easier to read; the matrix interface is useful in programmatic code. After validation, both resolve to the same numeric matrices and vectors.

Concept Data-frame interface Matrix interface
Localization covariates data plus x_cols X
One or many targets x0 or X0 x0 or X0
NP outcome y_col or y Y
CATE signal nuisance column names or pseudo_outcome pseudo_outcome
PLQR regressors D_cols D
PLQR nuisances g_col, mD_cols, density_col g, mD, density

Tibbles enter through the data-frame route; there is no separate tibble API. The package does not guess columns through nonstandard evaluation. Column names and their order are explicit parts of the call.

# Data-frame grammar
np_dnn(data = df, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), y_col = "Y", x0 = c(0, 0))

# Equivalent matrix grammar
np_dnn(X = as.matrix(df[c("X1", "X2")]), Y = df$Y, x0 = c(0, 0))

Continue with Getting started for a compact tour of the preferred interface, and Conditional Z-estimation for side-by-side estimator calls.

Estimator targets and signals

All four high-level wrappers localize with DNN weights, but they consume and return different statistical objects.

Wrapper Localized input Main returned target Interpretation
np_dnn() Outcome or scalar signal YiY_i mu Local conditional mean
cate_dnn() CATE pseudo-outcome ψi\psi_i tau Local conditional average treatment effect
plqr_dnn() Vector PLQR score ψi(θeval)\psi_i(\theta_{\mathrm{eval}}) moment; supplied theta Moment evaluation at a user-supplied coefficient
gmm_dnn() Model-defined vector moments gi(θ)g_i(\theta) solved theta Experimental local GMM estimate

The word score means an observation-level contribution. The word moment means its DNN-weighted average at a target. For scalar NP and CATE workflows, the weighted score is already the target estimate. For vector conditional moments, a localized moment must additionally be connected to a coefficient through evaluation or root solving.

Where package objects come from

Separating supplied quantities from computed quantities prevents several common misreadings of a fitted object. The table describes the high-level wrappers; lower-level weight and score tools expose more of the intermediate machinery.

Wrapper Supplied by the user Computed by RdistNN Main retained output
np_dnn() X, targets, and an outcome or signal DNN weights and their weighted mean mu, and se when requested
cate_dnn() X, targets, and either nuisance evaluations or a pseudo-outcome CATE signal when needed, then its DNN localization tau, and se when requested
plqr_dnn() X, targets, D, theta_eval, g, mD, and optionally density Scores and their local moment; Jacobian and sandwich pieces when inputs permit moment; supplied theta; separate moment- and coefficient-scale uncertainty fields
gmm_dnn() X, targets, a gmm_model, observed data, and model-specific nuisances Local moments, two-step root solving, weighting matrix, and sandwich pieces solved theta, se, vcov, and overidentification diagnostics

The package does not currently fit CATE, PLQR, or built-in IV-GMM nuisances. Those functions receive already evaluated nuisance vectors or matrices. Also note the asymmetry in theta: plqr_dnn() repeats a supplied evaluation value, whereas gmm_dnn() estimates a local root.

Continue with Conditional Z-estimation for the estimator workflows, or Extending RdistNN for the lower-level distance, rank-weight, and score layers.

Names that change meaning across estimators

Some short names are conventional within a model but are not package-wide synonyms. Interpret them together with the fitted-object class.

Name Meaning in one context Meaning elsewhere or important distinction
theta Supplied PLQR evaluation coefficient, copied into a plqr_result A coefficient solved separately at each target in a gmm_result
g The PLQR nonparametric shape nuisance g0(U)g_0(U) g_obs is the observation-by-moment contribution matrix in GMM, not a nuisance named g
J / jacobian jacobian is the derivative or bread matrix used for coefficient inference J in gmm_result is the scalar local overidentification statistic
se Target-scale standard error for NP, CATE, and GMM results PLQR uses moment_se and theta_se so the inferential scale is explicit
ess / neff / n_eff Three public spellings of inverse weight concentration None is a physical neighbor count or a radius diagnostic
score / moment An observation-level contribution versus its localized weighted average For scalar mean/CATE estimation the average is the target; for vector Z-estimation it may still require evaluation or solving

CATE nuisance conventions

cate_dnn() accepts one of three signal specifications.

Full AIPW signal

With outcome nuisances md(u)=𝔼[Y∣D=d,U=u]m_d(u)=\mathbb E[Y\mid D=d,U=u] and propensity e(u)=Pr⁡(D=1∣U=u)e(u)=\Pr(D=1\mid U=u), the package constructs

ψi=m1(Ui)−m0(Ui)+Di{Yi−m1(Ui)}e(Ui)−(1−Di){Yi−m0(Ui)}1−e(Ui). \psi_i = m_1(U_i)-m_0(U_i) +\frac{D_i\{Y_i-m_1(U_i)\}}{e(U_i)} -\frac{(1-D_i)\{Y_i-m_0(U_i)\}}{1-e(U_i)}.

The data-frame arguments are m0_col, m1_col, and e_col, together with y_col and t_col.

Robinson-form signal

With m(u)=𝔼[Y∣U=u]m(u)=\mathbb E[Y\mid U=u], the alternative signal uses m_col and e_col:

ψi={Yi−m(Ui)}{Di−e(Ui)}e(Ui){1−e(Ui)}. \psi_i = \frac{\{Y_i-m(U_i)\}\{D_i-e(U_i)\}} {e(U_i)\{1-e(U_i)\}}.

Precomputed pseudo-outcome

Users may instead provide pseudo_outcome directly. This is the only CATE signal route in the matrix interface. It is also the cleanest route when first-stage estimation is managed by another package or a cross-fitting pipeline.

The nuisance functions are supplied externally; cate_dnn() does not fit outcome or propensity models. It validates and clips supplied propensity values using clip, constructs the requested signal, and localizes that signal. Orthogonality of the score does not by itself certify the stability of an arbitrary same-sample nuisance learner.

Continue with Conditional Z-estimation for a worked CATE fit. For the paper-specific data-generating process and Monte Carlo harness, use Paper CATE simulation.

Experimental PLQR target and nuisance conventions

All PLQR functionality is experimental, including its scores, helpers, post-estimation methods, and plots. The initial release focuses on CATE and nonparametric regression; the PLQR API and inference interfaces may change.

For partially linear quantile regression, let DiD_i be the partially linear regressor and let UiU_i denote the full adjustment state. At a supplied coefficient theta_eval, plqr_dnn() forms the observation-level score

ψi(θeval)=[τ−𝟏{Yi≤Di⊤θeval+g0(Ui)}][Di−mD(Ui)]. \psi_i(\theta_{\mathrm{eval}}) = \left[ \tau- \mathbf 1\{Y_i\le D_i^\top\theta_{\mathrm{eval}}+g_0(U_i)\} \right] \left[D_i-m_D(U_i)\right].

The key names are deliberately literal:

  • theta_eval is the coefficient at which the moment is evaluated. plqr_dnn() does not solve for a new coefficient. Its returned theta repeats theta_eval at each target and records meta$theta_source = "supplied".
  • g or g_col supplies g0(U)g_0(U), the nonparametric shape component. It is not itself a conditional quantile; the threshold is D⊤θ+g0(U)D^\top\theta+g_0(U).
  • mD or mD_cols supplies mD(U)=𝔼[D∣U]m_D(U)=\mathbb E[D\mid U], used to form the residualized regressor D̃=D−mD(U)\widetilde D=D-m_D(U).
  • density or density_col supplies the positive conditional density of YY at the threshold. It enters the coefficient Jacobian, not the moment or its score-covariance meat.

These nuisances are supplied externally. They may depend on variables outside x_cols; RdistNN receives their evaluated values and does not fit or restrict their underlying models.

Moment diagnostics versus coefficient inference

This distinction is the most important PLQR reporting convention.

A localized vector moment can have a componentwise sampling diagnostic without supporting inference for a coefficient. In particular, moment_se describes the components of moment; by itself it does not estimate a coefficient standard error. Coefficient inference requires the full sandwich

V̂θ(x)=Ĵ(x)−1Ŝ(x)Ĵ(x)−⊤/neff(x). \widehat V_\theta(x) = \widehat J(x)^{-1} \widehat S(x) \widehat J(x)^{-\top} /n_{\mathrm{eff}}(x).

The PLQR routes are:

Requested route Bread Meat Coefficient inference fields
No density, jackknife enabled None Componentwise moment diagnostic moment_se only
density, theta_meat = "analytic" Density-backed jacobian Analytic score_covariance theta_se, theta_vcov, theta_omega
density, theta_meat = "jackknife" Density-backed jacobian Full delete-1 moment_vcov moment_se, moment_vcov, theta_se, theta_vcov, theta_omega

For the analytic route,

Ŝ(x)=τ(1−τ)∑iwi(x)D̃iD̃i⊤,Ĵ(x)=∑iwi(x)qiD̃iDi⊤. \widehat S(x) = \tau(1-\tau) \sum_i w_i(x)\widetilde D_i\widetilde D_i^\top, \qquad \widehat J(x) = \sum_i w_i(x)q_i\widetilde D_iD_i^\top.

For the jackknife-meat route, the full covariance moment_vcov replaces the analytic meat while the same density-backed Jacobian remains. The package does not reconstruct a coefficient covariance from the diagonal entries in moment_se; doing so would discard cross-moment covariance.

The coefficient fields have distinct scales:

  • theta_vcov is the finite-sample covariance used by confint() and predict(..., se.fit = TRUE);
  • theta_se is sqrt(diag(theta_vcov)) target by target;
  • theta_omega is the effective-sample-size-scaled covariance, theta_vcov * neff.

Direct coefficient inference requires normalized weights because the sandwich is defined for weight columns summing to one.

Continue with Conditional Z-estimation for the full PLQR call and with Diagnostics and reporting for Jacobian, conditioning, and field-availability diagnostics.

Experimental GMM conventions

gmm_dnn() is a separate, experimental front end. A gmm_model supplies a vector moment function, coefficient names, starting logic, and—when available—an analytic Jacobian. Unlike plqr_dnn(), gmm_dnn() solves for theta at each target using a two-step local GMM procedure.

Several names should not be transferred mechanically between the two APIs:

  • g is the PLQR shape nuisance, while g_obs in a gmm_result is the model-defined observation-level moment matrix.
  • jacobian is the derivative of the local moment map. The scalar J in a gmm_result is instead the local overidentification statistic.
  • omega is the estimated moment covariance entering the GMM weighting and sandwich calculation; vcov is the resulting coefficient covariance.
  • neff remains the DNN effective sample size.

Nuisance values required by a supplied gmm_model are also supplied externally. The package’s built-in doubly robust IV model validates those columns but does not fit them.

Continue with Local IV estimation for the experimental IV-GMM workflow. Use Extending RdistNN when the task is to define reusable score machinery rather than fit the built-in IV model.

Reading fitted objects

The core result fields are intentionally estimator-specific.

Class Point or moment fields Uncertainty fields Useful metadata
np_result mu se x0, meta$k, meta$s, meta$method
cate_result tau se x0, optional psi, optional nuisance
plqr_result moment, supplied theta, theta_eval moment_se or sandwich fields described above meta$theta_source, meta$theta_meat_method, neff
gmm_result solved theta, theta_first se, vcov; optional omega, jacobian J, df, pval_J, neff, convergence

Optional fields requested through return are additive. For example, asking for W, dx, ess, or tuning does not change the meaning of the main estimate. Use summary(), confint(), predict(), and diagnostics() where the fitted-object class documents those methods instead of inferring meaning from similarly named internal fields.

fit_cate$tau
fit_cate$se
diagnostics(fit_cate)

fit_plqr$moment
fit_plqr$theta_eval
fit_plqr$theta_se       # coefficient scale, when density was supplied
fit_plqr$moment_se      # moment scale; not a coefficient SE by itself

Continue with Diagnostics and reporting to see which diagnostics are structural, requested, or estimator-specific, and with Visualising fits to turn those fields into plots.

Practical reading checklist

When translating between a paper display and an RdistNN call, check the objects in this order:

  1. Identify the localization covariates X and target x0 or X0.
  2. Record s, k, the weight method, and whether weights are normalized.
  3. Identify the observation-level signal or vector score being localized.
  4. Mark every nuisance as supplied or package-computed. Current CATE, PLQR, and built-in GMM workflows expect nuisance values rather than fitting them.
  5. Determine whether the returned uncertainty is on the moment scale or the target-coefficient scale.
  6. Use n_eff/neff/ess as a scale and concentration diagnostic, not as a substitute for checking physical localization and first-stage assumptions.

The task table near the beginning of this article is the quickest route onward. For most analyses, the next stop is Conditional Z-estimation; return here when cross-estimator names or inferential scales become ambiguous.
